papers.title: "It Listens Better Than My Therapist": Exploring Social Media Discourse on LLMs as Mental Health Tool
papers.abstract: The emergence of generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT has prompted growing public and academic interest in their role as informal mental health support tools. While early rule-based systems have been around for several years, large language models (LLMs) offer new capabilities in conversational fluency, empathy simulation, and availability. This study explores how users engage with LLMs as mental health tools by analyzing over 10,000 TikTok comments from videos referencing LLMs as mental health tools. Using a self-developed tiered coding schema and supervised classification models, we identify user experiences, attitudes, and recurring themes. Results show that nearly 20% of comments reflect personal use, with these users expressing overwhelmingly positive attitudes. Commonly cited benefits include accessibility, emotional support, and perceived therapeutic value. However, concerns around privacy, generic responses, and the lack of professional oversight remain prominent. It is important to note that the user feedback does not indicate which therapeutic framework, if any, the LLM-generated output aligns with. While the findings underscore the growing relevance of AI in everyday practices, they also highlight the urgent need for clinical and ethical scrutiny in the use of AI for mental health support.

papers.title: Foundations of GenIR
papers.abstract: The chapter discusses the foundational impact of modern generative AI models on information access (IA) systems. In contrast to traditional AI, the large-scale training and superior data modeling of generative AI models enable them to produce high-quality, human-like responses, which brings brand new opportunities for the development of IA paradigms. In this chapter, we identify and introduce two of them in details, i.e., information generation and information synthesis. Information generation allows AI to create tailored content addressing user needs directly, enhancing user experience with immediate, relevant outputs. Information synthesis leverages the ability of generative AI to integrate and reorganize existing information, providing grounded responses and mitigating issues like model hallucination, which is particularly valuable in scenarios requiring precision and external knowledge. This chapter delves into the foundational aspects of generative models, including architecture, scaling, and training, and discusses their applications in multi-modal scenarios. Additionally, it examines the retrieval-augmented generation paradigm and other methods for corpus modeling and understanding, demonstrating how generative AI can enhance information access systems. It also summarizes potential challenges and fruitful directions for future studies.

papers.title: Reframing Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health Care: Toward a Human-Centered, Explainable, and Clinically Responsible Psychotherapeutic Paradigm
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Mental Health care represents a transformative shift in the diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment of psychological disorders. While AI-driven tools—including digital phenotyping systems, natural language processing models, and conversational agents—offer significant potential to enhance diagnostic precision, accessibility, and personalized interventions, they simultaneously introduce complex ethical, clinical, and epistemological challenges. This study provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of contemporary literature (2019–2025) to examine the ethical implications of AI deployment in psychotherapeutic contexts. Moving beyond descriptive review, the paper develops a conceptual ethical governance framework grounded in the principles of autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice, as well as the emerging “ethics of care” paradigm. It identifies key risk domains, including algorithmic bias, opacity of decision-making processes, data privacy vulnerabilities, erosion of therapeutic alliance, and the reconfiguration of professional accountability. Furthermore, the study proposes a human-centered, explainable, and clinically supervised AI integration model, emphasizing transparency, continuous ethical auditing, stakeholder inclusion, and hybrid human–AI decision-making structures. The findings highlight that while AI can significantly improve efficiency and expand access to mental healthcare—particularly in resource-constrained settings—its unregulated or poorly designed application may exacerbate inequalities, compromise patient autonomy, and undermine trust in clinical practice. The paper contributes to the interdisciplinary discourse by offering a structured ethical framework that bridges technological innovation with clinical responsibility and humanistic values. It concludes that sustainable and ethically aligned AI integration in mental health requires robust regulatory architectures, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and the preservation of the fundamentally human dimensions of psychotherapy.

papers.title: A Systematic Review on Artificial Intelligence-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems in Depression
papers.abstract: Purpose: This systematic review examines the current landscape of artificial intelligence (AI)-based Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) designed to aid in the treatment of depression. With depression recognized as a complex and multifactorial condition, often differing across contexts such as postpartum, adolescence, and elderly populations, the review aims to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and potential of AI-based CDSS in supporting personalized care. The primary research question explores how these systems are implemented and evaluated in clinical settings, as well as the main challenges to their broader adoption.Methods: The review analyzed studies focused on AI-based CDSS for depression, identifying variations in algorithms, performance metrics, and implementations. Studies were assessed based on system purposes, categorized into treatment selection, prediction and risk assessment, and clinical support and data review, providing a comprehensive overview of each study’s approach and outcomes.Results: 11 unique algorithms, 9 performance metrics, and 10 CDSS implementations were identified across the studies. Findings indicate positive results for CDSS in supporting clinical decision-making, yet highlight challenges in applying these tools in routine practice. Limitations include small, non-diverse sample sizes, immature methodologies, and difficulties in workflow integration, along with concerns about data privacy and the ethical use of AI.Conclusions: AI-based CDSS for depression shows potential in patient care; however, foundational issues such as more diverse samples and robust model development remain critical. Addressing these aspects will set the stage for future research into advanced applications, such as virtual-reality integration and multi-condition prediction, thus advancing AI’s role in mental health treatment.Clinical Relevance—This work illustrates the state of art of AI adoption in the domain of mental health, specifically in the context of depression.

papers.title: The application of AI-assisted music therapy tools in mental health interventions
papers.abstract: With the rising prevalence of mental health problems across populations, the limitations of traditional interventions have become more evident. Music therapy has received growing attention as a psychological intervention, and recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have created new opportunities for this field. This review examines the application potential and implementation pathways of AI-assisted music therapy tools for mental health interventions. Drawing on the literature and representative cases, this review summarizes application models and reported effects of AI in music therapy. The available evidence suggests that AI-assisted music therapy tools can support personalized interventions by adapting to users’ emotional and psychological states. Reported benefits include reductions in anxiety and depressive symptoms and improvements in emotion regulation across groups such as children, adolescents, and older adults. Finally, this review outlines priorities for future translation into mental health services and emphasizes data privacy and ethical standards to ensure responsible deployment.

literature_themes.theme: AI in Mental Health: Opportunities and Ethical Challenges
literature_themes.summary: This cluster examines the use of AI, particularly large language models and clinical decision support systems, in mental health care. Studies highlight benefits such as increased accessibility, emotional support, and personalized interventions, but also raise concerns about privacy, lack of professional oversight, algorithmic bias, and erosion of therapeutic alliance. User attitudes are generally positive, yet ethical governance frameworks are needed to ensure responsible deployment.
literature_themes.limitations: Key limitations include: reliance on self-reported user feedback without clinical validation; lack of standardized evaluation metrics for AI-based tools; insufficient integration of ethical frameworks in practice; and limited evidence on long-term efficacy and safety across diverse populations (e.g., postpartum, adolescent, elderly).
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster reveals gaps in: (1) rigorous clinical trials comparing AI tools to traditional therapy; (2) development of explainable AI models that preserve therapeutic alliance; (3) privacy-preserving data sharing mechanisms; and (4) culturally adaptive AI interventions. These gaps can guide future research on responsible AI integration in mental health.

literature_themes.theme: Foundations of Generative AI for Information Access
literature_themes.summary: This cluster focuses on how generative AI models, through large-scale training and superior data modeling, transform information access systems. It identifies two key paradigms: information generation (creating tailored content) and information synthesis (integrating existing knowledge). The chapter covers foundational aspects like architecture, scaling, training, and applications in multi-modal scenarios, including retrieval-augmented generation.
literature_themes.limitations: The cluster does not fully address model hallucination in synthesis tasks, scalability issues in real-world deployment, and potential biases in generated content. It also lacks empirical comparisons with traditional IA systems.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights gaps in mitigating hallucination, improving grounding in external knowledge, and evaluating generative IA in diverse domains. It supports identifying research opportunities in robust retrieval-augmented generation and multi-modal integration.

summary: The literature highlights AI's potential in mental health care through tools like large language models, clinical decision support systems, and music therapy, offering benefits such as increased accessibility, personalized interventions, and emotional support. However, significant challenges remain, including ethical concerns (privacy, bias, lack of oversight), limited clinical validation, and gaps in long-term efficacy across diverse populations. Foundational work on generative AI for information access underscores the need for robust, explainable, and ethically governed systems to ensure responsible deployment.
gap: How can AI-based clinical decision support systems for depression be rigorously evaluated in randomized controlled trials across diverse populations (e.g., postpartum, adolescent, elderly) to establish long-term efficacy and safety compared to standard care?
question: How can AI-based clinical decision support systems for depression be rigorously evaluated in randomized controlled trials across diverse populations (e.g., postpartum, adolescent, elderly) to establish long-term efficacy and safety compared to standard care?
hypothesis: AI-based clinical decision support systems for depression will demonstrate non-inferiority in reducing depressive symptoms compared to standard care in a randomized controlled trial across postpartum, adolescent, and elderly populations, with sustained effects at 12-month follow-up.
methodology: A multi-site, parallel-group, superiority randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing an AI-based CDSS for depression (e.g., treatment recommendation algorithm) plus treatment-as-usual (TAU) vs. TAU alone. Participants will be recruited from three distinct populations: postpartum women (n=150), adolescents aged 13-17 (n=150), and elderly aged 65+ (n=150). The primary outcome is change in depression severity (PHQ-9) at 6 months, with secondary outcomes at 12 months. Blinding of outcome assessors and data analysts will be implemented. The CDSS will be integrated into electronic health records with clinician oversight. Sample size calculations will account for attrition and subgroup analyses.
proposal: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into mental health care, particularly through clinical decision support systems (CDSS), holds promise for improving depression treatment by enhancing accessibility and personalization. However, existing literature reveals a critical gap: the lack of rigorous, long-term randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating AI-based CDSS across diverse populations, such as postpartum women, adolescents, and the elderly, while also addressing ethical concerns like explainability and clinician oversight. To address this, we propose a multi-site, parallel-group, non-inferiority RCT comparing an explainable AI-based CDSS (providing treatment recommendations with confidence scores and rationale) plus treatment-as-usual (TAU) versus TAU alone across three distinct populations (n=200 each, powered at 80% to detect a non-inferiority margin of 2 points on PHQ-9, assuming 20% attrition). The primary outcome is change in depression severity (PHQ-9) at 12 months, with secondary outcomes at 6 and 18 months. We hypothesize that the AI-CDSS will be non-inferior to standard care in reducing depressive symptoms, with sustained effects at follow-up. The CDSS will be integrated into electronic health records with a standardized clinician override protocol and continuous ethical auditing as per Paper 3's framework. Unlike prior studies that focus on narrow populations or short-term outcomes, our design incorporates diverse populations, long-term follow-up, and explainability features, directly addressing gaps identified in Papers 1, 3, and 4. Expected contributions include establishing evidence for AI-CDSS effectiveness and safety, informing ethical guidelines, and providing a replicable evaluation framework. Key limitations include potential lack of generalizability beyond the three populations, inability to blind participants and clinicians, and reliance on self-reported outcomes.
draft_proposal: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into mental health care, particularly through clinical decision support systems (CDSS), holds promise for improving depression treatment by enhancing accessibility and personalization. However, existing literature reveals a critical gap: the lack of rigorous, long-term randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating AI-based CDSS across diverse populations, such as postpartum women, adolescents, and the elderly. While prior studies have demonstrated AI's potential in symptom monitoring and therapy support, they often suffer from small sample sizes, short follow-up periods, and limited generalizability. To address this, we propose a multi-site, parallel-group, superiority RCT comparing an AI-based CDSS (providing treatment recommendations) plus treatment-as-usual (TAU) versus TAU alone across three distinct populations (n=150 each). The primary outcome is change in depression severity (PHQ-9) at 6 months, with secondary outcomes at 12 months. We hypothesize that the AI-CDSS will demonstrate non-inferiority to standard care in reducing depressive symptoms, with sustained effects at follow-up. This study extends prior work by incorporating rigorous blinding, sample size calculations accounting for attrition, and subgroup analyses to assess efficacy across age and life-stage groups. Expected contributions include establishing evidence for AI-CDSS effectiveness and safety, informing ethical guidelines, and providing a replicable evaluation framework. Unlike previous research focusing on narrow populations or short-term outcomes, our design directly addresses the need for robust, generalizable evidence to support responsible AI deployment in mental health.

proposal_critique.clarity_issues: The problem definition is clear but could be more specific about the type of AI-CDSS (e.g., treatment recommendation algorithm) and the comparator (TAU is vague). The hypothesis states non-inferiority, but the design is described as superiority RCT, creating confusion.
proposal_critique.logic_issues: There is a mismatch between the hypothesis (non-inferiority) and the stated design (superiority RCT). The hypothesis should match the design (e.g., superiority or non-inferiority). Also, the gap and question focus on rigorous evaluation, but the proposal does not specify how the CDSS recommendations are implemented or how clinician oversight is standardized.
proposal_critique.novelty_issues: The proposal claims novelty by including three diverse populations and long-term follow-up, but similar multi-population RCTs exist in the literature (e.g., Paper 4 calls for diverse samples). The novelty is incremental; the proposal should articulate a unique contribution, such as a novel adaptive algorithm or integration of explainability features.
proposal_critique.methodology_issues: The sample size of 150 per group is not justified with power calculations. Attrition is mentioned but not quantified. Blinding is limited to outcome assessors and analysts; participants and clinicians cannot be blinded, introducing bias. The primary outcome at 6 months may be too short for long-term efficacy claims. The CDSS integration into EHR is mentioned but not detailed (e.g., how alerts are delivered, how clinicians override).
proposal_critique.literature_alignment_issues: The proposal aligns with gaps identified in Papers 1, 3, and 4 (need for RCTs, diverse populations, ethical oversight). However, it does not address the ethical framework from Paper 3 (e.g., explainability, human-centered design) or the generative AI foundations from Paper 2 (e.g., hallucination risks). The proposal should incorporate these to strengthen scholarly positioning.
proposal_critique.academic_depth_issues: The proposal lacks depth in discussing theoretical underpinnings (e.g., why AI-CDSS might work differently across populations), mechanisms of action, and potential confounders. It does not address how the CDSS handles missing data, model updates, or adverse events. The ethical considerations are mentioned only superficially.
proposal_critique.revision_plan: Clarify the design as a non-inferiority RCT and align hypothesis accordingly. Provide a power analysis with attrition estimates. Detail the CDSS algorithm, including its training data, explainability features, and clinician override protocol. Incorporate ethical safeguards from Paper 3 (e.g., continuous auditing, patient consent for AI use). Add a theoretical framework explaining expected differential effects across populations. Specify how the CDSS will be integrated into clinical workflow and how fidelity will be monitored.

rubric_scores.justification: The proposal clearly defines the research problem (lack of rigorous RCTs for AI-based CDSS in depression across diverse populations), motivation (addressing gaps in literature), target users (postpartum, adolescent, elderly), and proposed solution (multi-site non-inferiority RCT with explainable AI). Implications for ethical guidelines and clinical practice are explicitly discussed.

The proposal logically flows from literature analysis to gap identification, hypothesis generation, method design, and evaluation planning. Each stage is clearly connected: literature themes reveal gaps, gap leads to hypothesis, hypothesis informs RCT design, and evaluation metrics align with outcomes. Transitions are explicit.

The proposal is meaningfully distinct: it addresses the lack of long-term, multi-population RCTs for AI-based CDSS, incorporates explainability and ethical auditing (from Paper 3), and proposes a non-inferiority design with 12-month follow-up. This goes beyond prior short-term, single-population studies.

The design is realistic: multi-site RCT with three populations, clear sample sizes (n=200 each, powered for non-inferiority), primary and secondary outcomes, blinding of assessors, and integration with EHR. Risks (attrition, blinding limitations) are acknowledged. However, details on recruitment strategies, data management, and cost estimates are missing, preventing full marks.

The proposal is strongly grounded in retrieved papers: it cites gaps from Papers 1, 3, and 4, uses the ethical framework from Paper 3, and addresses limitations of prior work (short-term, narrow populations). It clearly explains how the proposal extends existing research.

The proposal demonstrates mature academic thinking: verifiable hypothesis, rigorous methodology (RCT with non-inferiority design), awareness of limitations (generalizability, blinding, self-report), and theoretical grounding in ethical frameworks. It moves beyond summarization to propose a novel evaluation paradigm.
Writing is clear, concise, and professional. Sections are well organized, terminology is consistent, and the proposal is easy to follow. Citations are appropriately integrated.

evaluation.comments: The proposal is well-structured, novel, and feasible, with strong alignment to the literature. Minor improvements could include more detailed recruitment and cost plans.

Clinics are randomized to implement an AI-based CDSS for depression at different time points. Participants include all adult patients with depression (no age restriction). Primary outcome: depression remission rate at 6 months (PHQ-9 <5). Secondary outcomes include safety events, patient satisfaction, and clinician adherence. The stepped-wedge design allows all clinics to eventually receive the intervention, enhancing ethical acceptability. Analysis uses mixed-effects models accounting for clustering and time.
candidates.reason: Pragmatic design improves generalizability but does not specifically target diverse populations as per hypothesis; stepped-wedge may complicate long-term follow-up and increase logistical complexity.

Participants are stratified by population (postpartum, adolescent, elderly) with 100 per arm per stratum (total N=900). Primary outcome: change in depressive symptoms (HAM-D) at 12 months. Secondary outcomes include quality of life, adverse events, and therapeutic alliance. The design includes a run-in period to ensure CDSS usability. Analysis uses ANCOVA with stratification factors and multiple imputation for missing data.
candidates.reason: Strongest design with three arms, stratification, and long-term follow-up, but low feasibility due to large sample size, high cost, and complexity of implementing AI alone without oversight.
